case_info.scenario: A woman in her mid-20s was evaluated for a history of dyspnea on exertion for 2 years. On physical examination, her pulse was 70 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg. The cardiovascular examination showed a loud S1, normal S2, and an opening snap along with a mid-diastolic, soft, rumbling murmur at the apex of the heart. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left atrial enlargement. The echocardiogram showed severe mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2with a mean (SD) gradient of 20 (4) mm Hg. There was no evidence of any subvalvular thickening, leaflet calcification, or mitral regurgitation. The patient was taken for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV). A 6F pigtail catheter was placed in the left ventricle via the right femoral artery. The interatrial septum was punctured using a Mullins sheath and Brockenbrough needle via the right femoral vein. Entry into the left atrium was made and confirmed with a dye injection. However, suddenly, the patient developed acute onset of dyspnea along with retrosternal chest pain. Her blood pressure at the time of the event was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96%. The catheter was pulled back into the right atrium, and chest fluoroscopy was performed (Figure;Video).

case_info.answer: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position
case_info.caption: The fluoroscopy image of the patient at the time of dyspnea.
case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

1. Mental Demand

case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is

            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two

            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

case_info.scenario: A woman in her mid-20s was evaluated for a history of dyspnea on exertion for 2 years. On physical examination, her pulse was 70 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg. The cardiovascular examination showed a loud S1, normal S2, and an opening snap along with a mid-diastolic, soft, rumbling murmur at the apex of the heart. Entry into the left atrium was made and confirmed with a dye injection. However, suddenly, the patient developed acute onset of dyspnea along with retrosternal chest pain. case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

case_info.answer: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position
case_info.caption: The fluoroscopy image of the patient at the time of dyspnea.
case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

case_info.answer: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position
case_info.caption: The fluoroscopy image of the patient at the time of dyspnea.
case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.

   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

     message imposes on YOU.

       the case?"

       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.answer: 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position
case_info.caption: The fluoroscopy image of the patient at the time of dyspnea.
case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left atrial enlargement. The echocardiogram showed severe mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2with a mean (SD) gradient of 20 (4) mm Hg. There was no evidence of any subvalvular thickening, leaflet calcification, or mitral regurgitation. The patient was taken for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV). A 6F pigtail catheter was placed in the left ventricle via the right femoral artery. The interatrial septum was punctured using a Mullins sheath and Brockenbrough needle via the right femoral vein. Entry into the left atrium was made and confirmed with a dye injection. However, suddenly, the patient developed acute onset of dyspnea along with retrosternal chest pain. Her blood pressure at the time of the event was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96%. The catheter was pulled back into the right atrium, and chest fluoroscopy was performed (Figure;Video).

case_info.scenario: A woman in her mid-20s was evaluated for a history of dyspnea on exertion for 2 years. On physical examination, her pulse was 70 beats per minute, and blood pressure was 110/70 mm Hg. The cardiovascular examination showed a loud S1, normal S2, and an opening snap along with a mid-diastolic, soft, rumbling murmur at the apex of the heart. The electrocardiogram showed normal sinus rhythm with left atrial enlargement. The echocardiogram showed severe mitral stenosis with a mitral valve area of 0.9 cm2with a mean (SD) gradient of 20 (4) mm Hg. There was no evidence of any subvalvular thickening, leaflet calcification, or mitral regurgitation. The patient was taken for balloon mitral valvotomy (BMV). A 6F pigtail catheter was placed in the left ventricle via the right femoral artery. The interatrial septum was punctured using a Mullins sheath and Brockenbrough needle via the right femoral vein. Entry into the left atrium was made and confirmed with a dye injection. However, suddenly, the patient developed acute onset of dyspnea along with retrosternal chest pain. Her blood pressure at the time of the event was 100/60 mm Hg, pulse was 70 beats per minute, and oxygen saturation was 96%. The catheter was pulled back into the right atrium, and chest fluoroscopy was performed (Figure;Video).

case_info.explanation: Air embolism in main pulmonary D. 100% Oxygen, intravenous fluid, and Trendelenburg position The fluoroscopy of the patient at the onset of dyspnea showed a pulsatile translucency in the main pulmonary artery (MPA). The shape of the opacity was similar to the trunk of the MPA and showed alternating expansion and contraction during the cardiac cycle. The opening and closing of the pulmonary valve were visible at the inferior part of the translucent shadow (Figure;Video). This was diagnosed as a large pulmonary artery air embolism in the MPA. Pericardial effusion leading to pericardial tamponade is a rare complication of BMV. However, acute tamponade is accompanied by hypotension. Also, on fluoroscopy, tamponade will appear as a decreased movement of cardiac borders along with separation of visceral and parietal pericardium due to accumulation of blood, which was not present in this case. Hence, pericardiocentesis was not indicated. Acute massive pulmonary thromboembolism in the MPA gives rise to acute-onset hypotension and dyspnea, but fluoroscopy is usually unremarkable. Rarely, fluoroscopy may show a prominent pulmonary artery, an enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla sign), an abrupt cutoff of vessels, elevated hemidiaphragm along with focal pulmonary oligemia (Westermark sign), and peripheral, pleural-based, wedge-shaped opacity (Hampton hump) due to pulmonary infarction. Acute pulmonary embolism appears as a filling defect on contrast angiography rather than on fluoroscopy. As none of these features was present, intravenous thrombolytic and catheter-directed embolectomy were not indicated in this patient. Massive pulmonary artery air embolism was previously described among patients who were undergoing pacemaker implantation.1The most common risk factors for air embolism during an intervention are dehydration, low central venous pressure, coughing, deep inspiration, old age, use of a large central venous sheath, and deep sedation. The symptoms of an air embolism can be asymptomatic to life-threatening depending on its size.2If an air embolism occurs with resulting hypotension, cardiopulmonary resuscitation should be started immediately. Patients should be given 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids, along with inotropic support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation as needed.2Recently, the Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus position) has been described for the management of air embolism in preference to the Trendelenburg position. In rare cases, the use of a catheter has been described for the suction of air from the pulmonary artery.3 The BMV procedure was stopped immediately, and the patient was placed in the Trendelenburg position and started treatment with 100% oxygen and intravenous fluids. A decision was made to remove the air in the MPA using Judkins right coronary catheter, but the air embolus was absorbed within 3 to 4 minutes with the medical management alone. The patient quickly recovered and was discharged in stable condition. She was advised to return after 1 month for the BMV.
